title: After-School Care Inside Senior Living Communities
angle: Pairing 2: Mental health, loneliness and community x Parenting, childcare deserts and kids/AI/screens
one_liner: Turn senior living's empty afternoon dining rooms into licensed school-age programs where residents are reading, repair and garden 'buddies', funded by parent tuition, operator economics and loneliness-intervention budgets.
customer: Working parents of K-5 kids near independent- and assisted-living communities (dependent-care FSA eligible, cap $7,500). Secondary payers: senior living operators seeking occupancy and retention, and Medicare Advantage plans or Area Agencies on Aging funding loneliness programs.
problem: The 3-6pm care gap is where parents lose work hours, and average US childcare costs $13,128 (35% of income for single parents). Older adults are the least-served, highest-need loneliness segment, and 40-46% of adults 65+ are 'unsure' about AI companions (Pew, Aug 2026), so a human alternative has open ground. Operators have empty spaces between lunch and dinner and no scalable, reimbursable engagement model.
solution: 'Bridge Clubs': the community lends the room 2:30-6pm. We run a licensed school-age program (1:12 ratio, bus drop from the elementary school). Residents opt into structured 30-minute roles ('Reading Elders', 'Tinkerers', 'Garden Crew'). We track participation and a loneliness scale (UCLA-3) monthly and package the data for MA plans and AAAs so they can fund resident engagement. Parents pay less than typical after-school rates because space and volunteer time subsidize it.
why_now: The dependent-care FSA cap rose to $7,500 and the 45F employer childcare credit rose to 40% (50% for small businesses) in 2026, opening employer and parent budgets. WHO's 2025 Commission put loneliness on the health agenda. Payers are hunting for measurable loneliness interventions, and school-age licensing is lighter than infant care in many states.
revenue_model: Parent tuition of about $325-475/mo. Operator rent-share or management fee. Engagement-based fees from MA plans or AAAs. Employer sponsorship of slots via the 45F credit.
non_obvious_insight: This is two 'deserts' each holding the other's unused capacity. 'Intergenerational programming' usually fails as charity. It works when the payer stack (tuition, operator occupancy, and loneliness reimbursement) makes it profitable and the resident role is a job, not a photo op.
first_30_days: Find three independent-living operators within a mile of Title I elementary schools with after-school waitlists. Run a 6-week pilot with 12 kids in one dining room using a licensed partner provider. Charge $99 registration plus $349/mo. Collect resident participation and UCLA-3 scores. Take the data to one regional MA plan's community benefits team.

title: Fry-Oil Co-op Escaping Evergreen Renderer Contracts
one_liner: Aggregate independent restaurants' used cooking oil, sell it to biofuel buyers at market with sensor-verified traceability, and hand the owner the check the big renderer keeps.
customer: Independent restaurants and small chains with 2-20 fryer-heavy units are the supply side and pay no fee. Local independent oil collectors, biodiesel, renewable diesel and SAF feedstock processors and brokers are the demand side and pay the co-op. Revenue is the spread plus a small sensor rental fee.
problem: Used fry oil is a commodity that biofuel makers have been bidding up, yet independents are locked into 3-year auto-renewing pickup contracts with a large renderer or bin company. The restaurant is paid a pittance or nothing, or is even charged fees. Bins overflow, which brings health-code and odor problems. Thieves steal oil at night, and nobody reconciles what the oil is actually worth. Owners don't switch because the termination window is a 60-90 day certified-letter deadline buried in the contract, and nobody has time to run a bid.
solution: A co-op platform that: (1) tracks each member's contract renewal date and files the non-renewal notice on time; (2) runs a monthly reverse auction among local collectors so that volume, not the restaurant, gets the price; (3) installs a roughly $40 ultrasonic fill sensor and a lockable tank cap, so pickups trigger at 80% full and every pickup is photo- or QR-verified; (4) issues a statement per pickup indexed to a published used-cooking-oil price series; and (5) produces per-restaurant chain-of-custody records that renewable-fuel producers need to prove domestic, traceable feedstock.
why_now: As I understand it, federal clean-fuel incentives (45Z) now favor North American feedstock, and concern about mislabeled imported used oil has raised the value of traceable domestic oil. Renewable diesel and SAF capacity keeps growing. Cheap cellular fill sensors are widely available. Restaurants' margins are so thin that any found cash gets attention. Verify the current feedstock price index and the 45Z sourcing rules before you pitch.
revenue_model: 20-30% spread on oil sold, indexed and transparent, plus $10-30 per month for the sensor and tank lock. Later add a premium for verified-traceable oil sold to fuel producers, and carbon-intensity documentation fees.
non_obvious_insight: The incumbent's real product is the locked contract and route density, not the oil service, so the way in is the calendar rather than a better price. The contract renewal date is the CRM key: a 90-day-out certified non-renewal letter, filed for the owner, is the growth engine. Owners think they are getting 'free removal', so nobody shops it. Also, per-restaurant traceability is worth more to fuel buyers than the oil's volume alone.
first_30_days: Walk one restaurant row and photograph each bin's contract label, and note the pickup company and renewal date for 40 restaurants in one metro. Sign one local collector or small biodiesel maker as a buyer with a written price index. Enroll 8-10 off-contract or month-to-month members, including my own two locations. Install sensors and lock caps, run the first monthly auction, and show each owner a side-by-side statement of what their old vendor paid versus what the co-op did.

title: N-of-1 Trial Network for the Peptide Boom
one_liner: IRB-supervised, blinded, randomized N-of-1 trials that let peptide users learn what works for them while building the missing evidence base.
customer: Consumers already using or considering BPC-157, TB-500, GHK-Cu or KPV (pay ~$249 per 12-week trial), plus clinics, 503A pharmacies, wearable and supplement brands that need substantiation.
problem: Peptides are legal-ish again (HHS Feb 2026; FDA panel Jul 23, 2026 backed BPC-157 and KPV despite agency concerns), yet there is no evidence base. Users self-experiment uncontrolled, clinics cannot substantiate claims, and the FDA panel itself flagged the gaps.
solution: A 503A pharmacy ships coded vials (active vs placebo, randomized crossover), an app collects pre-registered endpoints (pain scores, sleep, grip strength, wearable HRV) plus baseline and 8-week safety labs, and Bayesian analysis returns each person's answer and contributes to a public aggregated dataset. Start with BPC-157 for tendon and joint pain.
why_now: Peptide deregulation in 2026, cheap wearables and remote endpoints, AI-assisted protocol design and statistics, and a crowd of volunteers already injecting. N-of-1 designs need tens of people per question, not hundreds.
revenue_model: $249 per participant, $50-150k sponsor-funded studies from clinics and brands, and data licensing.
non_obvious_insight: When regulation retreats, credible evidence becomes the scarce good. The crowd already volunteers, and pre-registered N-of-1 series can outrun a traditional RCT for low-risk, subjective-endpoint questions.
first_30_days: Draft protocol and IRB submission with an FDA IND-exemption determination from counsel. Recruit ~60 people through biohacker communities and one partner clinic. Line up a 503A pharmacy for blinded placebo and open a $249 waitlist for the first cohort.

title: Age-Tier Compliance for Roblox-Style Creator Studios
one_liner: Pre-flight scanner and consulting that checks user-generated game experiences against Roblox Kids (<9), Select (9-15) and 16+ tier rules before discovery demotion costs revenue.
customer: UGC studios and creators earning $200k-$10M a year on Roblox and similar platforms (Fortnite UEFN), plus brand agencies commissioning sponsored experiences.
problem: Roblox mandated age checks (Jan 2026) and split into Kids, Select and standard tiers in June 2026. Experiences now must match a tier on chat, random-reward purchases, ads, voice and data collection. Misclassified experiences lose tier-based discovery. Indonesia's ban also covers Roblox. Studios don't understand how classification works and brand clients fear child-privacy liability.
solution: A 'tier lint' tool that combines public metadata with scripted play-throughs to flag features that clash with each tier, gives a fix list (for example, disable free text in Kids, replace loot boxes) and produces a 'brand-safe by tier' report for sponsors. A public changelog tracks platform policy changes.
why_now: The tier split is only three months old and the rules are still moving. Toy and media brands (Mattel's games push, per the brief) are commissioning kids' UGC experiences, and state attorney-general suits against Roblox (from memory) raise brand caution.
revenue_model: Subscription at $500-3k a month per studio, plus $5-15k audits for brand-sponsored experiences.
non_obvious_insight: Tiering turns content rating into distribution: the platform's discovery algorithm becomes the regulator, and the UGC studio, not Roblox, eats the cost of getting it wrong. That is a classic compliance-consultancy niche, like Amazon seller-policy work.
first_30_days: Scrape metadata on the top 500 experiences. Identify about 30 likely mis-tiered ones. Send each studio owner a personalized mini-audit. Sell 10 audits at $1.5k. Start a public policy-change newsletter to build trust.

title: Satellite Cannibalization Scores for Rural ISP Lenders
one_liner: Address-level risk scores that show which rural ISP portfolios LEO broadband will hollow out, and which it will not.
customer: Lenders to rural ISPs (cooperative and agricultural lenders, community banks), funds buying wireless or fiber ISPs, tower and fixed-wireless investors, and state broadband offices that allocate subsidies.
problem: Starlink went from 8.9M to 12M subscribers in six months (per the briefing) while ARPU fell 19% in one quarter. That means it is pricing down into the rural segments small ISPs live on. Lenders still underwrite these ISPs on legacy subscriber-count assumptions, and nobody can tell which locations are actually exposed.
solution: A data product that scores every serviceable location: fiber or cable alternatives, fixed wireless, LEO availability and price, local congestion, and expected churn or ARPU pressure. It rolls up to portfolio covenants, valuation adjustments and acquisition due-diligence reports. Updated monthly as satellite pricing and capacity change.
why_now: Subscriber growth of about 35% in six months, falling ARPU and satellite eligibility in subsidy programs all landed in 2025-26. Starship-driven capacity growth should push prices down further.
revenue_model: Portfolio subscription $2-10k per month per lender. $10-40k per acquisition due-diligence report. Data licensing to ISP-focused funds.
non_obvious_insight: The consensus is fiber wins and satellites lose. The actual exposure is mid-density fixed-wireless and DSL footprints, and the difference is visible at address level. Lenders get paid for knowing which side of that line each loan sits on.
first_30_days: Build a prototype on public availability maps, FCC broadband data and published Starlink plan tiers for three states. Pitch five agricultural or community lenders with a free look at one real portfolio. Convert one to a paid pilot.

title: Package Travel Surcharge Compliance for Tour Operators
one_liner: A rules engine that calculates lawful fuel-driven price increases on already-sold package tours, generates the notices and tracks the 8% cancellation trigger.
customer: Small and mid-size EU and UK package organisers, coach-tour and cruise-package sellers, and agents acting as organisers with EUR 5-200M in sales, plus their bonding insurers.
problem: With the Hormuz closure and soaring jet fuel, packages sold months ago are underwater and airlines are cutting capacity and raising fares. Under EU and UK package rules an organiser can raise prices only if the contract allows it, only for fuel, tax or exchange-rate changes, with at least 20 days' notice, and an increase above 8% lets travellers cancel free. Organisers must also pass on decreases. Spreadsheet errors mean refunds and regulator complaints.
solution: Connect to booking exports, model the cost components per trip, compute the lawful pass-through per contract clause, and generate localised notices with timelines. Track the 8% threshold and deadlines, keep an audit trail for regulators and bonding insurers, and flag contracts whose clauses need rewriting.
why_now: Iran declared the Strait of Hormuz closed on 2 Mar 2026 and, by September, budget carriers cite soaring fuel costs with capacity cuts and fare hikes ahead. Shorter booking lead times (33 days versus 37.5) do not help packages sold long in advance.
revenue_model: EUR 300-1,500 per month per operator or about 0.1% of sales, plus per-notice fees and clause redesign consulting.
non_obvious_insight: In a cost shock much of the loss is legal rather than commercial. Operators eat costs because they misread pass-through limits or send defective notices, so compliance software turns panic into recovered margin.
first_30_days: Build a calculator and notice templates in a spreadsheet plus an LLM. Publish a gated '2026 fuel surcharge playbook' through trade associations, and sell 10 operators at EUR 500 per month.

title: Genki Tap: Konbini Clerks as Paid Elder Watchers
one_liner: Pay convenience-store staff to log a three-second 'seen and how they seemed' note on enrolled elderly regulars, and alert family and local support centers when someone goes quiet or drifts.
customer: Adult children living outside Osaka with a widowed or single parent in the city, at about ¥1,480 a month. Later customers are municipal community support centers (chiiki hokatsu shien centers) paying per enrolled senior, and eventually banks, trust banks and insurers that need early cognitive-decline and fraud signals.
problem: In 2025, 76,941 people died alone at home in Japan, 58,919 of them aged 65 or older. The Cabinet Office estimates about 22,222 were found after 8 or more days. Municipalities have signed 'elder-watching network' MOUs with konbini, post offices and newspaper carriers, but they are unpaid goodwill. The clerk notices, if that clerk happens to be on shift and cares, and the observation never becomes structured data. Owners know who has not come in for three days. We notice the customer buying the same item twice in a day, paying slowly with coins, forgetting the wallet, or getting confused at self-checkout. None of it reaches the family or the ward.
solution: The senior gets a keychain NFC tag or simply says a name. At the register, staff tap a ¥1,500 reader or a tablet and press one of three buttons: fine, a bit off, worried. If an enrolled senior is not seen for 48-72 hours, the system messages the family and a designated neighbor, then the local support center. The family gets a weekly digest such as 'came Mon, Wed, Thu; usual purchases; once forgot wallet'. The store earns ¥300-500 per enrolled senior per month, so the attention is paid for and survives shift changes. Consent is opt-in, data is minimal, and the escalation path runs through licensed care managers.
why_now: The National Police Agency now publishes annual solitary-death counts, and the 2025 figures show no decline. Municipalities are legally responsible for loneliness and isolation measures under the 2024 loneliness law. Post-2024 summer heat deaths at home have raised demand from families. Cashless and prepaid-card fraud aimed at seniors is also rising, so a clerk who already knows the customer is the best front-line filter.
revenue_model: Family subscription of ¥1,480 a month, of which ¥300-500 goes to the store. Municipal or support-center contracts pay per enrolled senior. Later, anonymized cognitive-drift signals feed paid programs from banks, trust companies and insurers concerned about dementia-related frozen assets and fraud.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource in elder monitoring is not sensors or AI, it is a trusted human who sees the person daily and is already 24/7 in the neighborhood. Municipal networks fail because the clerk's attention is unpaid and unstructured. A ¥300 payment plus a three-button interface turns free goodwill into reliable, recurring, auditable data. The store that sees the drift first is the konbini, not the clinic.
first_30_days: Enroll 8-10 owners in Ikuno, Nishinari, Higashinari and Abeno wards, starting with my own three stores. Use a LINE OA for families and cheap NFC readers or a phone app for staff. Identify 30 regulars whose adult children live in Tokyo, Nagoya or Fukuoka and pitch them by phone; aim for 50 paying families at ¥1,480. Sign an MOU with one community support center as the escalation partner. Log every alert and outcome so the pilot produces evidence for a municipal contract.

title: Disordered-Eating Tripwire for GLP-1 Prescribers
one_liner: A cheap, documented eating-disorder screen and escalation network embedded in GLP-1 telehealth intake.
customer: White-label medical groups that supply prescribers to many telehealth brands, GLP-1 telehealths, med spas and their malpractice carriers.
problem: GLP-1 use was ~50% among binge-eating-disorder patients and ~42% among atypical anorexia patients (JAMA Psychiatry 2026), and an NEJM 2026 perspective warned about masking and worsening disordered eating in telehealth. An investigation tied four white-label medical groups to ~30% of telehealth firms receiving FDA warning letters, and MDL 3094 has 4,700+ cases pending. Plaintiff lawyers and boards look for the next vector, and no screening or monitoring layer exists.
solution: A 3-minute validated screen (SCOFF or EDE-Q short form) inside intake, 2-question monthly check-ins, rules-based escalation to a network of ED-trained dietitians and therapists, and an exportable audit trail for boards and insurers.
why_now: FDA sent 30 letters in Mar 2026 and 25 in Jun 2026. Regulators, boards and carriers are moving to documented safeguards. The data showing high GLP-1 use in eating-disorder populations is new in 2026.
revenue_model: $3-6 per screened patient, $40-80 per escalation (paid by the prescriber or referral network), and a malpractice-carrier discount program.
non_obvious_insight: In white-label telehealth, liability concentrates in the medical group that sits behind dozens of brands, so a cheap, documented safeguard is standard-of-care insurance. ED providers also need referral flow, so escalation pays for itself.
first_30_days: Pitch two mid-size white-label groups or a 20k-patient telehealth. Deliver via an embeddable link, run 500 screens, and publish flag-rate benchmarks. Recruit 10 ED-trained clinicians for escalation.

title: Restaurant Kitchens as Chefs for Small Care Homes
one_liner: License a turnkey program that lets restaurants use dead hours to cook dietitian-approved, texture-modified meals for 6-20 bed assisted-living and adult-family homes that big foodservice ignores.
customer: Operators of small licensed residential care homes (adult family homes, board-and-care, personal care homes, small RCFEs) pay per resident per day, typically $8-12 for lunch and dinner. Adult children pay for premium 'chef-cooked' upgrades. The restaurant is the supplier, and the platform takes a license fee and revenue share.
problem: In a small care home, food is the main daily pleasure and the top resident complaint, yet it is cooked by overworked caregivers from warehouse-club and broadline food, with little variety and hard-to-manage special diets (mechanical soft, pureed, low-sodium, diabetic). Sodexo and Compass do not serve 6-bed homes and meals-on-wheels serves people at home. Meanwhile my kitchens sit idle from 2 to 5pm and on slow days, my cooks want more hours, and my dine-in traffic is soft.
solution: A meal program in a box for restaurants: a rotating 5-week menu library with dietitian sign-off and texture-modified variants (IDDSI levels), allergen and diet labels, batch-cook and cook-chill (or same-day hot delivery) SOPs, a state-specific health-department pre-clearance checklist and HACCP plan templates, routing and billing software, and a contracted registered dietitian on retainer. The restaurant cooks in dead hours and delivers 2-3 times a week in labeled pans, and the care home reheats. Ten homes at about $17-22k per year each is $170-220k of found revenue at healthy contribution margin on capacity that was previously idle.
why_now: The 65+ population is growing fast (the 'Peak 65' wave runs through about 2027). Families are shifting to small, cheaper residential homes rather than large assisted-living campuses. Restaurant dine-in traffic has been soft and owners are actively looking for non-traffic revenue. Kitchen labor is short, and steady off-peak hours help retention. Public state license lists make the small-home buyer easy to find. I couldn't verify current home counts this session, so pull the licensing-list counts state by state before building.
revenue_model: Onboarding fee of $1-2k per restaurant, plus 10-15% of meal revenue, plus software billing at about $100 per month per restaurant. Optional premium tier for adult-child paid 'chef upgrades' and dietitian services.
non_obvious_insight: The gold is in the mismatch between an idle asset and an ignored customer. Small-home operators are often immigrant nurses and caregivers running a tiny business with no procurement power, and no large foodservice company will serve them, but a two-location restaurant can absorb a 300-meal-per-week route into dead hours at nearly zero marginal labor cost. What a restaurant cannot do alone is the compliance layer (texture modification, diet labeling, dietitian review, regulator pre-clearance), and that is the product.
first_30_days: Pull the state's public list of small residential care homes and shortlist 30 within a 15-minute drive. Call my health department to confirm what is required to supply prepared meals from a licensed restaurant to a licensed facility. Hire a freelance registered dietitian by the hour for one 2-week menu. Offer 3 homes a free trial week, then convert them at about $9 per resident per day. Document the SOPs and the regulator's answer as the first version of the product.

title: Quality-of-Earnings Audits for Robot Fleets
angle: Pairing 2: Logistics and physical automation x Trust and verification markets (lens: audits)
one_liner: A finance-native auditor that verifies deployed units, productive hours, teleoperation share and revenue per robot for the lenders, lessors and investors underwriting robot, AV and drone fleets.
customer: Lenders, equipment lessors, SPAC sponsors, growth funds and acquirers underwriting robotics, AV and drone companies. Second wave: insurers of AV trucks and warehouse robots, and investors in robot-as-a-service lease pools.
problem: Robotics valuations run on self-reported fleet metrics. Agility reported $1.8M of 2025 revenue against a $2.5B SPAC. Maven raised $100M with about 8 robots deployed. Serve booked about $1.3k of revenue per robot. Figure reports about 740 robots against about 600 employees. 1X NEO's early demos were largely teleoperated. Nobody audits 'deployed' vs 'productive' vs 'autonomous' vs 'paid'. AV insurers price 'slightly above' human trucks on the unknown, and lessors cannot underwrite $499-$600/mo robot leases blind.
solution: A boutique assurance firm. Under NDA it gets read-only telemetry, remote-assist logs and billing, and visits sites. It produces a signed Fleet QoE report with standard metrics: units deployed vs productive hours, human interventions per robot-hour, revenue and margin per unit, safety events, uptime and maintenance cost, and contract quality. Later, publish a standard 'Fleet Passport' for covenant reporting.
why_now: About 22,000 humanoids shipped in H1 2026. Unitree IPO'd in Aug 2026. Agility is going public via SPAC. Figure plans a $600/mo lease. Skild ($14B) and Physical Intelligence ($11B) are priced for perfection. Leasing and asset-backed structures for robots are being invented now, and capital allocators need evidence, not demos.
revenue_model: $40k-$120k per diligence engagement, buyer-paid. $10k-$30k per year of continuous covenant monitoring for lenders and lessors. An anonymized benchmark data license to insurers.
non_obvious_insight: The metric that decides whether a robotics company is a software business or a labor-arbitrage business, hidden human-intervention hours per robot-hour, is invisible to the buyer. Capital allocators, not vendors, must be the payer, because vendor-paid attestation fails (Trustpilot was fined for selling to those it rates). An ex-assurance plus ex-robotics team beats a technical certifier.
first_30_days: Write a 40-item data request and an intervention-hour analysis template. Recruit an ex-Big-4 assurance lead and one robotics ops engineer. Offer two free pilot audits to a debt fund or equipment lessor with a robot deal in progress. Publish an anonymized 'what to ask a robotics CEO' metrics guide. Aim for one paid engagement letter within 60-90 days.

title: Lend Against Battery Earnings for Vet Bills
angle: Pairing 2: Energy transition & the grid x Pets & animal health
one_liner: A wallet that routes VPP and demand-response payouts into a dedicated pet-care fund, then advances emergency vet money against the battery's telemetry-verified future earnings.
customer: Home-battery owners in VPPs (repayment via payout offset). Partners who pay are VPP aggregators and retail energy providers (retention) and pet insurers (customer acquisition).
problem: Vet bills are lumpy and emotional: 85% of vet professionals say clients decline care at estimates of $1,000 or less, and 13% of euthanasias are attributed to inability to pay. Only about 5% of US dogs and cats are insured, while premiums rose 19.7% against 9% growth in insured animals, which invites churn. High-APR deferred-interest cards are the fallback. Meanwhile VPP payouts are small, abstract and easily ignored, even though dispatch is real (580 MW from 140,000 California batteries on September 9, 2026).
solution: Owners assign payouts to a Pet Reserve that auto-pays insurance premiums and pre-funds vet bills at partner clinics. Once the balance builds, they can draw an advance repaid from future dispatch payments, underwritten on battery telemetry and contracted programs. Start with credits and premium payments only, and add advances through a bank or lender partner once the data is proven.
why_now: VPPs are now large enough to have contracted, metered payout streams (Base Power raised $1B with a 500+ MWh fleet; Sunrun/Tesla dispatch). Pet insurance repricing is pushing owners to look for offsets, and no aggregator owns a consumer-finance layer.
revenue_model: Referral bounty from pet insurers ($50-150 per policy), retention/SaaS fee from aggregators or retailers, and interest or fee spread on repayable advances via a lending partner.
non_obvious_insight: A battery in a VPP is a telemetry-verified income stream, and it is collateralizable. Converting abstract kWh payouts into 'vet visits' also changes how much owners value flexibility, and the pet emergency is the highest-emotion, lowest-friction use of the credit.
first_30_days: Recruit one small VPP operator or retail energy provider (not Tesla) and 300-500 pet-owning households through battery-owner communities. Launch payout-to-Pet-Fund with premium auto-pay and a referral deal with one insurer. Measure opt-in, retention and how many households use the balance for vet bills. Hold advances until a lending partner and legal review are in place.

title: Warranty-Linked Installer Certification for African Solar Batteries
angle: Education, credentialing and skills after AI x Emerging markets leapfrogging
one_liner: Battery and inverter brands pay per certified installer and per registered installation, and every certification requires geotagged commissioning proof, which builds an installed-base registry that lenders and insurers cannot otherwise get.
customer: Battery and inverter brands and their distributors in Nigeria, Kenya and Ghana (and Indian rooftop and backup-power distributors), paying about $8-15 per registered install plus certification event fees. Asset lenders and insurers pay later for registry data. Installers pay $15-25 for the badge.
problem: Africa has imported more battery dollars than panel dollars from China since 2024, and 75% of solar growth is distributed. Ember estimates its numbers are 2x the official statistics, and only 14 of 54 countries reported 2025 data. Bad installs (loose lugs, undersized cable, misconfigured battery communications) drive warranty costs and fires. Brands cannot tell who installed what and where. Lenders and insurers cannot price the risk.
solution: A 2-day practical certification in a rented workshop with real inverters, batteries and torque tests, run by senior local installers. After certification, every job requires a geotagged photo checklist and serial scans through a WhatsApp or lightweight app flow, and the brand's warranty desk validates instantly. In return installers get faster claims, brand lead flow and pricing power. Trainees come from underemployed electrical-engineering graduates and, reportedly, technicians returning from Gulf jobs.
why_now: Africa is installing about 17 GW in 2026 (+45% year on year), with batteries now the larger import dollar. The Hormuz-linked energy shock and diesel costs push more households and shops toward backup power. India's induction-cooktop rush (reported 20-25x demand) is stressing home wiring and backup systems. Official statistics cannot see any of it, so private registries have unusual value.
revenue_model: $8-15 per registered install from the brand, $1-3k per certification event, and $15-25 badge fees from installers. Lenders and insurers pay $20-60k a year for registry access, or per-lookup fees.
non_obvious_insight: The certification is the data-collection mechanism. Nobody can sell a registry to a lender directly, but every installer will sign up for a badge that speeds warranty claims, and the registry is exhaust from that. It fixes the exact blind spot Ember describes, and the payer at the start is the brand with a warranty bill, not the trainee.
first_30_days: Pick Lagos or Nairobi. Sign one distributor of a top-five battery brand as the pilot payer, using its own warranty-claim cost as the case. Rent a workshop and certify 30-40 installers on day one, with the distributor covering $20 per head. Use WhatsApp plus a form tool with serial-number OCR and no custom code. Target 300 registered installs in 90 days and show the brand the change in its claim rate.

title: The Junior Bench: Rent-a-Resident for AI Review
one_liner: Mid-size accounting, legal and insurance firms rent trained new grads for 12 weeks to verify their AI-produced work, rebuilding the vanished junior rung as a paid residency.
customer: Regional accounting firms, boutique law firms, insurance brokerages and healthcare revenue-cycle companies; new grads join as paid residents.
problem: Employers stopped hiring juniors because AI does the grunt work, yet they still need future seniors. AI-exposed majors have 5 points lower initial employment, grads are 42% underemployed, and 22-25 year-olds in exposed jobs are 19% below trend. Meanwhile firms carry liability for AI-drafted work that nobody is trained to verify well.
solution: A cohort residency. Two weeks of domain and AI-verification training, then about ten weeks embedded in the firm's workflow reviewing AI-drafted workpapers, contract abstracts or claims against sources, with seeded-error scoring. The firm pays a weekly rate and can convert residents to hires. Each resident builds a scored 'verification record' that becomes the credential.
why_now: Payroll data show a widening hiring gap since August 2025. Firms are AI-first but facing quality and liability incidents, and partner pipelines will look empty in about five years.
revenue_model: About $1,800-2,500 per resident-week from the firm against roughly $900-1,100 wage cost, giving 40-50% gross margin. Optional conversion fee if hired early.
non_obvious_insight: AI did not remove the junior job; it turned it from doing into checking. Checking is a trainable, measurable skill with an obvious buyer: the firm that carries the liability for AI errors.
first_30_days: Sell to 3 regional CPA firms ahead of busy season with 5 residents each. Recruit from local accounting grads. Build an error-injection test set to score residents. Charge from week one.

title: Baseline: Bank-Feed Proof of Displacement Costs
one_liner: An app that reconstructs a displaced family's 'normal' spending from pre-loss bank statements and computes the exact increase that Additional Living Expense coverage owes, in carrier-ready format.
customer: Public adjusters and disaster-recovery nonprofits (paying per file), and carriers or TPAs handling long-tail displaced-household claims (paying per active ALE file per month). Consumers use it free.
problem: ALE pays the increase over normal living costs, not the total, so proving it requires a baseline that almost no family has. Adjusters spend hours rebuilding it from memory and shoeboxes, families under-claim (groceries, laundry, mileage, pet boarding, storage, higher utilities) or document sloppily, and disputes turn ugly. With California's new smoke-damage law (AB 1795, effective Jan 1, 2027) barring insurers from cutting off ALE until the home is restored, thousands of standing-home households will run ALE claims for years with heavy documentation demands.
solution: A privacy-first tool that ingests 12 months of pre-loss bank or card data (via open-banking link or uploaded statements), builds a per-category baseline, then diffs it month by month against post-loss spending, matches receipts, and flags gaps the family can legitimately claim (extra mileage, meal delta, rented furniture, storage). Output is an ALE ledger with audit trail in the format desk adjusters actually accept, plus a deadline tracker for policy ALE time limits. Processing is on-device or in a private enclave, and the data is deleted after export.
why_now: More than 13,000 standing-home smoke claims from the Eaton and Palisades fires are still unresolved 20 months later, a lawsuit accuses Farmers' vendor of substandard assessments, and AB 1795 makes ALE duration a live issue. LLM parsing of messy statements and receipts is now cheap and accurate enough to be a product. Carriers are cutting adjusters (entry-level postings down about 50% since 2025) but ALE files still need documentation, so automation that delivers clean files is welcomed.
revenue_model: Public adjusters and recovery groups pay $99-$199 per file. Carriers and TPAs pay $30-$60 per active ALE file per month, or $75-$150 per closed file, in exchange for fewer touches and fewer complaints. Optional referral fees from moving, storage and rental-furniture vendors for legitimate, claimable purchases.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody in the industry records 'normal.' The claim's central number, the increase over normal, is unmeasured on the policyholder's side, and adjusters know most under-claiming is not a coverage denial but the family's inability to prove what they used to spend. Bank data is the only pre-loss record the insured always has.
first_30_days: Build a prototype that categorizes statement CSVs and PDFs into ALE categories and produces a monthly delta ledger. Offer it free to 10 Altadena and Palisades public adjusters and to two survivor-support networks in exchange for feedback and 20 anonymized-consent pilot files. Ask two carrier ALE desk managers to review the output format and sign a paid pilot at $50 per file for 200 files. Prepare a privacy policy and data-deletion promise, because trust is the product.

title: Solar Battery Warranty-Claim Recovery Desk
one_liner: Pool failed-battery claims from small African installers and enforce them against Chinese manufacturers for a share of recovered value.
customer: Solar installers and importers in Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana and South Africa holding failed batteries and inverters.
problem: Africa has imported more battery dollars than panels from China since 2024. Cheap packs fail, and claims need serial verification, BMS logs, RMA logistics and language skills, so installers absorb the losses.
solution: A claims desk that captures failure evidence by QR and app, files with OEMs, consolidates returns and tracks credit notes. The wedge is five Lagos importers with a backlog of dead units.
why_now: The battery import surge of 2024-26 is now reaching failure age, and installer margins are compressing.
revenue_model: 15-25% of recovered value, moving to SaaS plus failure-data sales to insurers.
non_obvious_insight: A warranty is worth only what you can enforce. Batching many small buyers gives leverage over OEMs and produces failure data that insurers need.
first_30_days: Collect backlog lists from three importers and file the first 100 claims.

title: Publish the Obvious: Generative Prior Art vs. Patent Thickets
one_liner: Turn cheap AI generation into a defensive weapon by industrially publishing dated, enabling disclosures of every obvious variant around a product, so secondary 'evergreening' and troll patents can't be granted.
customer: Primary: generic and biosimilar manufacturers and public-interest funders (procurement agencies, health-access NGOs) facing secondary patent thickets on drugs losing primary protection. Secondary: hardware, robotics and protocol-foundation startups afraid of patent trolls.
problem: Secondary patents on dosing regimens, polymorphs, formulations, devices and manufacturing tweaks extend monopolies long after the core compound expires, and they are cheap to file, especially now that AI drafts applications. Challengers' tools (IPR, oppositions, litigation) are expensive and come after the patent issues. Startups have no defense budget against troll assertions.
solution: A pipeline in which LLMs plus a patent agent or PhD reviewer enumerate the design space around a target product: formulations, dose schedules, salt and crystal forms, delivery devices, process variations. It drafts enabling defensive disclosures and timestamps them. It deposits them where examiners actually search (IP.com Prior Art Database, Research Disclosure, plus DOI-bearing repositories such as Zenodo and ChemRxiv that patent-office non-patent-literature tools crawl). It then monitors new filings, maps which disclosures block which claims, and files third-party submissions where the law allows. Sold as a per-product 'novelty shield' with measurable outcomes: examiner citations and rejections.
why_now: Compound patents on semaglutide and other blockbuster GLP-1s are expiring in several large markets in 2026, triggering a stampede of generic entry and follow-on patent strategies. LLMs now make it cheap to enumerate enabling variants at scale. Patent offices are swamped and revising guidance on AI-assisted work, and nobody has industrialized the defensive side of the novelty game.
revenue_model: $15-80k per product-family shield for generics and funders; $500-2k/month subscriptions for startups and foundations; success-based bonuses when a filing is rejected citing a disclosure; grant and NGO funding for public-health targets.
non_obvious_insight: Prior-art status depends on what was publicly and enablingly disclosed, not on who or what wrote it. So when generating variations is free, the asymmetric weapon is to publish the space before anyone can claim it. The scarce thing is no longer ideas but credible, discoverable, dated publication. It also aligns the incentive: the parties who pay (generics, health funders) gain directly from the commons staying open.
first_30_days: Pick 3 products with visible secondary-patent thickets and imminent generic entry. Produce about 200 enabling disclosures per product, each reviewed by a contracted patent agent. Publish to two or three searchable indexes. Send free 'thicket map' reports to 5 generic makers and 2 access-focused funders. Sell the first shield for $15-25k. Track later filings to prove examiner citations. Have patent counsel vet the approach up front, including that every disclosure is actually enabling and accurate.

title: PFAS Test-Result Exchange for Small Brands
one_liner: A members' data pool where small brands share lab results indexed by supplier, material lot and SKU, so nobody pays $500+ to test the same fabric or coating twice.
customer: Product-compliance managers at small and mid-size apparel, outdoor, cookware, cosmetics, textile and food-packaging brands and importers ($5M-$200M revenue) selling into US states with PFAS product laws and into the EU.
problem: PFAS rules are fragmenting through state product bans and reporting laws, EU packaging limits and a pending EU universal restriction (all unverified in the briefing; re-check current status). Supplier declarations fail because suppliers often do not know what is in their coatings. Testing costs hundreds of dollars per sample, and small brands that buy from the same mills and coaters each test alone. 'PFAS-free' marketing claims also draw class actions.
solution: A neutral cooperative. Members upload lab PDFs, which are parsed automatically and tagged to supplier, mill, material spec and date. The exchange scores confidence per supplier-material ('3 independent labs, 12 samples, all under threshold'), flags outliers, recommends where a new test buys the most certainty per dollar, negotiates group lab rates, and generates the state or EU evidence file. Contributions earn credits.
why_now: State PFAS product deadlines and EU packaging PFAS limits are landing in 2025-26 (background, verify), total-fluorine screening is cheap enough to run routinely, and LLM parsing turns messy lab PDFs into structured data.
revenue_model: Membership of $3-15k/year by revenue tier, pay-per-query for non-contributors, a 10-15% margin on group lab testing, and a paid 'independently verified' badge program.
non_obvious_insight: Declarations fail through ignorance, not malice, so the durable defense is measurement. Measurement is a shared-cost, non-competitive good, like a credit bureau for materials. Antitrust risk is low if the pool holds test data only and never pricing.
first_30_days: Partner with one accredited lab and one trade association (outdoor or apparel). Recruit 10 founding members who contribute 200+ historical lab reports, stand up a spreadsheet-backed MVP with parsed PDFs, and charge a $2.5k founding fee.

title: Transformer Buying Co-op for Small Utilities
one_liner: Pool the orders of hundreds of rural co-ops and municipal utilities into one standardized spec so they can get in line together.
customer: Roughly 900 electric distribution co-ops and 2,000 municipal utilities, plus solar and storage developers. They pay a procurement fee.
problem: Power transformer lead times average 128 weeks, distribution transformer prices are up as much as 95%, and over 40M units are past service life. Small utilities order in dozens with bespoke specs and go to the back of the line. One contrarian says standardized units can ship in 12-14 months, so procurement, not manufacturing, is the bottleneck.
solution: Pre-negotiated framework agreements with two or three manufacturers (including offshore) for a small menu of standard units, for example pad-mount 25-167 kVA and 5-10 MVA substation units. Add a predictive replacement list built from age and AMI loading data, a financed rotating stock pool, and slot reassignment among members.
why_now: Data centers outbid utilities for manufacturing slots, lead times are at 128 weeks, and co-ops and munis are scrambling with no purchasing leverage.
revenue_model: 2-4% procurement fee, a stock-pool financing and storage spread, and $10-30k a year SaaS for replacement planning.
non_obvious_insight: Part of the shortage is fragmentation. Manufacturers prioritize buyers who commit to standard specs and volume, and small utilities are collectively huge but individually invisible.
first_30_days: Collect 30 co-op and muni transformer spec sheets. Propose a common spec at a state co-op association or APPA event. Get five utilities to sign LOIs for a 200-unit pilot order. Talk to two mid-size manufacturers with open 2028 slots.

title: Peer-Made Aide Training in Creole, Spanish, Tagalog
angle: Pairing 1: Aging & silver economy x Creator economy / AI provenance
one_liner: A library of short scenario videos made by experienced home-care aides in their own languages, RN-reviewed and sold to agencies as required in-service training that keeps new aides from quitting.
customer: Home-care agencies, home health agencies and nursing homes in immigrant-heavy states (NY, FL, MA, NJ, CA). The buyer is the training or HR lead, paying per aide.
problem: Agency turnover runs 77-80% and roughly 4 in 5 new caregivers quit within 100 days. 30% of direct care workers are immigrants (60% in New York), and about 350,000 Haitians lost TPS on Aug 4. Federal rules require annual in-service hours for home health aides and nursing-home nurse aides (12 hours a year, and states add more), and most content is English-language corporate e-learning or AI-dubbed avatars that workers ignore and that can be clinically wrong.
solution: Recruit working aides who already post in Haitian Creole, Spanish, Tagalog or Arabic on Facebook, TikTok and WhatsApp. They shoot 3 to 6 minute scenarios (transfers, dementia redirection, refusing a bath, safe lifting). An RN reviews each script, and the clip carries a 'peer-made, RN-verified' provenance stamp. The platform adds quizzes, attendance logs for surveyors, and a first-week mentor-video track aimed at the 100-day cliff. Creators get 35-40% of revenue plus a bonus for completion.
why_now: Visa pauses and TPS terminations are reshuffling the workforce by language group right now. The federal nursing-home staffing mandate was repealed (Feb 2026), which leaves retention as the agencies' only lever. AI slop training content is flooding the market, and creators are hunting for income beyond ad revenue.
revenue_model: $9-14 per aide per month billed to the agency (a 75-aide agency pays about $700-1,000), sold as an annual contract. About 35-40% goes to creators. A later add-on covers state-approved CE credits and dementia-training modules.
non_obvious_insight: Aides do not quit because training is bad. They quit because nobody who looks or sounds like them says the job gets easier. A peer in your language who has survived the first 100 days is a retention device that also happens to satisfy a compliance line item, and an AI avatar cannot supply that credibility.
first_30_days: Find 5 aide-creators through Creole, Spanish and Tagalog Facebook groups and workforce training programs. Partner with a per-diem RN reviewer. Shoot 20 scenarios in 3 weeks and pitch 5 agencies (start with Miami, Boston and NYC) on a 90-day pilot at a free-first-month price tied to a measured 100-day retention improvement.

title: GLP-1 Stipend-in-a-Box for Small Employers
one_liner: A counsel-reviewed HRA wrapper that lets small employers subsidize $149-$299 cash-pay GLP-1s with a capped monthly stipend.
customer: Employers with roughly 10-200 employees, sold through brokers, PEOs and HRA administrators.
problem: Large-employer coverage fell from 72% to 60% and more are dropping, while 27% of employers already point staff to LillyDirect or NovoCare. Direct-to-employer vendors like Waltz Health and 9amHealth target mid and large plans. Small employers can't carve out of a fully insured plan, and stipend plans raise ERISA, ACA and tax questions they can't answer.
solution: A packaged structure (QSEHRA, ICHRA or limited-purpose HRA, depending on group size) with plan documents, capped stipend rules, receipt-based reimbursement from DTC pharmacies, minimum-essential-coverage checks, and optional coaching. Brokers get a commission.
why_now: $149-$299 manufacturer cash prices make a capped stipend cheaper than open-ended coverage. Employers just dropped or plan to drop coverage before open enrollment, and TrumpRx and DTC channels launched in 2026.
revenue_model: $5-8 per employee per month plus ~5% of stipend flow, with broker commission share.
non_obvious_insight: The fight is over who administers the wrapper for the 90% of employers that PBM carve-out vendors don't serve. Compliance and broker distribution matter more than the coaching content.
first_30_days: Have an ERISA attorney draft the plan documents. Partner with an existing QSEHRA or HRA administrator. Pilot with 10 small employers (~300 lives) through two brokers and measure uptake and cost per participant.
